propositions.text: Mrs. Khan is a Pakistani citizen whose permanent residence application was denied due to her spouse's inadmissibility for crimes against humanity.
propositions.quote: The Applicant, Mrs. Khan, is a citizen of Pakistan. Her application for permanent residence in Canada was denied after her spouse was found to be inadmissible to Canada on the basis that there are reasonable grounds to believe that he had been complicit in the commission of crimes against humanity, and that he had personally participated in such crimes when he was a high-ranking member of Pakistan’s military.

paragraphs.summary: Mrs. Khan is a Pakistani citizen whose permanent residence application was denied due to her spouse's inadmissibility for crimes against humanity, court states.

propositions.text: Mrs. Khan argues the decision denying her application lacks sufficient justification, transparency, and intelligibility.
propositions.quote: Mrs. Khan asserts that the decision denying her application should be set aside on the basis that the reasons provided were not sufficiently justified, transparent or intelligible.

paragraphs.summary: Mrs. Khan argues the decision denying her application lacks sufficient justification, transparency, and intelligibility.

propositions.text: The application is dismissed; the court disagrees with Mrs. Khan's assertion.
propositions.quote: I disagree. For the reasons that follow, this Application will be dismissed.

paragraphs.summary: The court disagrees with Mrs. Khan and dismisses the application.

propositions.text: Mrs. Khan disclosed her spouse's military service from 1976 to 2000, reaching Lieutenant Colonel rank, in her investor class application.
propositions.quote: In support of her application for permanent residence in Canada as a member of the investor class, Mrs. Kahn disclosed that her spouse had been employed with Pakistan’s military between 1976 and 2000, and that he had risen through the ranks to eventually become a Lieutenant Colonel.

paragraphs.summary: Mrs. Khan disclosed her spouse's military service and rank in her investor class application, court states.

propositions.text: Mr. Khan acknowledged membership in the joint Pakistani military and police Field Interrogation Team during Operation Clean Up and use of certain interrogation techniques.
propositions.quote: A summary of the Interview states that Mr. Khan acknowledged that he had been a member of the joint Pakistani military and police Field Interrogation Team [FIT] in Karachi when it was involved in “Operation Clean Up” in 1992 and 1993; and that he had used interrogation techniques such as slapping, punching, using stress positions and forcing detainees to look at the sun, during that period.

propositions.text: Mr. Khan insisted these techniques did not constitute torture as no severe methods causing long-term damage were used.
propositions.quote: That summary added that Mr. Khan insisted that those techniques did not constitute torture because no electricity, water boarding, heavy beatings or techniques that caused long-term physical damage were used.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker found Mr. Khan acknowledged his role in interrogation techniques but denied they constituted torture.

propositions.text: The visa office lacked a transcript of the Interview but included a redacted CSIS security advice brief in the record.
propositions.quote: The visa office in London, U.K., informed former counsel to Mrs. Khan that it did not have a transcript of the Interview. However, a redacted version of the security advice brief of the Canadian Security Intelligence Services [CSIS] security advice brief was included at pages 235–239 of the Certified Tribunal Record [CTR].

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker noted no interview transcript but included a redacted CSIS security advice brief in the record.

propositions.text: Mr. Khan clarified he did not personally use or condone interrogation techniques but acknowledged they legally constitute torture.
propositions.quote: Through counsel, Mr. Khan subsequently clarified that he had not personally used or witnessed such interrogation techniques, that he does not personally condone them and that he suspects the police alone had used them. However, he acknowledged that such techniques would legally constitute torture (CTR, at 205, 212 and 218).

paragraphs.summary: Mr. Khan clarified he did not personally use or condone interrogation techniques but acknowledged their legal classification as torture.

propositions.text: The Decision under review includes a form letter and computerized notes prepared by the Immigration Officer and others involved.
propositions.quote: The decision under review [the Decision] is comprised of a form letter, dated January 7, 2016, and computerized notes [Notes] that were prepared by the Immigration Officer [the Officer] who issued the Decision, as well as by others who were involved in processing Mrs. Khan’s application.

propositions.text: The parties agree the Notes form part of the Decision.
propositions.quote: It is common ground between the parties that the Notes form part of the Decision.

paragraphs.summary: The Decision includes a form letter and notes prepared by the Immigration Officer and others, agreed by parties to be part of the Decision.

propositions.text: The letter informed Mrs. Khan her application was rejected because her spouse is inadmissible under IRPA paragraph 35(1)(a).
propositions.quote: The letter informed Mrs. Khan that her application for a permanent resident visa had been rejected on the basis that there are reasonable grounds to believe that her spouse, Muhammad Asif Khan, is a member of the inadmissible class of persons described in paragraph 35(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c 27 [IRPA].

propositions.text: Under IRPA paragraph 42(1)(a), a foreign national is inadmissible if an accompanying or prescribed non-accompanying family member is inadmissible.
propositions.quote: The letter explained that, pursuant to paragraph 42(1)(a) of the IRPA, a foreign national is inadmissible on grounds of an inadmissible family member if their accompanying family member or, in prescribed circumstances, their non-accompanying family member is inadmissible.

propositions.text: Since her spouse is inadmissible, Mrs. Khan is also inadmissible.
propositions.quote: Given that her spouse is inadmissible, she too is inadmissible.

paragraphs.summary: The letter explained Mrs. Khan's application was rejected because her spouse is inadmissible, making her inadmissible under IRPA.

propositions.text: The Decision described Mr. Khan's military service and his statements about interrogation techniques.
propositions.quote: Among other things, the Decision described the facts relating to Mr. Khan’s military service and the statements that he allegedly made regarding the interrogation techniques that he used, as described at paragraph 5 above.

propositions.text: The Decision described Mr. Khan's clarifications but found them insufficient to reconsider his inadmissibility.
propositions.quote: The Decision also described the subsequent clarifications that were provided by Mr. Khan. However, the Officer stated that those responses did not appear to be sufficient to warrant a reconsideration of Mr. Khan’s inadmissibility.

paragraphs.summary: The Decision described Mr. Khan's military service and clarifications but found them insufficient to reconsider inadmissibility.

propositions.text: The Decision referred to open-source reports of military human rights abuses in Pakistan, including torture.
propositions.quote: In addition, the Decision referred to open-source information that reported upon human rights abuses, including torture, perpetrated by the military in Pakistan.

propositions.text: The Decision stated Mr. Khan was a member of army divisions responsible for human rights abuses including torture.
propositions.quote: The Decision further stated that Mr. Khan had been a member of divisions within the army which were responsible for human rights abuses, including torture.

propositions.text: Given Mr. Khan's lengthy voluntary military service, the Officer concluded he was complicit in reported human rights abuses during his service.
propositions.quote: Given the length of Mr. Khan’s military service, and the fact that it had been voluntary, the Officer concluded that he would have been complicit in the human rights abuses reported to have been committed by the military during the time that he was in its service.

paragraphs.summary: The Decision found Mr. Khan complicit in military human rights abuses including torture due to his voluntary service.

propositions.text: IRPA paragraph 42(1)(a) deems a foreign national inadmissible if an accompanying or prescribed non-accompanying family member is inadmissible.
propositions.quote: As noted above, paragraph 42(1)(a) of the IRPA provides that a foreign national, other than a protected person, is inadmissible on grounds of an inadmissible family member if that person’s accompanying family member or, in prescribed circumstances, their non-accompanying family member, is inadmissible.

paragraphs.summary: IRPA paragraph 42(1)(a) makes a foreign national inadmissible if an accompanying or prescribed non-accompanying family member is inadmissible.

propositions.text: IRPA paragraph 35(1)(a) deems a person inadmissible for committing crimes against humanity under CAHWCA sections 4 to 7.
propositions.quote: Pursuant to paragraph 35(1)(a) of the IRPA, a permanent resident or foreign national is inadmissible on grounds of violating human or international rights where that person has committed an act outside Canada that constitutes an offence referred to in sections 4 to 7 of the Crimes Against Humanity and War Crimes Act, SC 2000, c 24 [CAHWCA].

paragraphs.summary: IRPA paragraph 35(1)(a) deems a person inadmissible for crimes against humanity under CAHWCA sections 4 to 7.

propositions.text: IRPA section 33 includes facts for inadmissibility based on reasonable grounds to believe facts have occurred or may occur.
propositions.quote: Pursuant to section 33 of the IRPA, the facts that constitute inadmissibility under sections 34 to 37 include facts arising from omissions and, unless otherwise provided, include facts for which there are reasonable grounds to believe that they have occurred, are occurring or may occur.

paragraphs.summary: IRPA section 33 includes facts for inadmissibility based on reasonable grounds to believe facts have occurred or may occur.

propositions.text: CAHWCA subsection 6(1) criminalizes crimes against humanity, including torture under subsection 6(3).
propositions.quote: Among other things, subsection 6(1) of the CAHWCA provides that every person who, either before or after the coming into force of that provision, commits a crime against humanity is guilty of an indictable offence. Pursuant to subsection 6(3), a crime against humanity includes torture.

paragraphs.summary: CAHWCA subsection 6(1) criminalizes crimes against humanity, including torture under subsection 6(3).

propositions.text: CAHWCA subsection 7(1) criminalizes military commanders who fail to prevent or report crimes against humanity by subordinates.
propositions.quote: Pursuant to subsection 7(1) of the CAHWCA, a military commander commits an indictable offence if that person, outside Canada, fails, before or after the coming into force of that section, to exercise control properly over a person under their effective command, or control or effective authority and control, and as a result the latter person commits an offence under section 6. Subsection 7(1) creates an additional offence where a military commander knows, or is criminally negligent in failing to know, that the person described immediately above is about to commit or is committing such an offence. In each case, the offence is not complete unless the military commander (i) fails to take, as soon as reasonably practicable, all necessary and reasonable measures within their power to prevent or repress the commission of the offence, or the further commission of the offence; or (ii) fails to take, as soon as practicable, all necessary and reasonable measures within his or her power to submit the matter to the competent authorities for investigation and prosecution.

paragraphs.summary: CAHWCA subsection 7(1) criminalizes military commanders who fail to prevent or report crimes against humanity by subordinates.

propositions.text: CAHWCA subsection 7(2) establishes similar offences for superiors other than military commanders.
propositions.quote: Subsection 7(2) of the CAHWCA establishes similar offences for a “superior,” who is defined to be “a person in authority, other than a military commander.”

paragraphs.summary: CAHWCA subsection 7(2) establishes similar offences for superiors other than military commanders.

propositions.text: Full text of relevant provisions is provided in Appendix 1 to these reasons.
propositions.quote: The full text of the aforementioned provisions is provided in Appendix 1 to these reasons.

paragraphs.summary: Full text of relevant provisions is provided in Appendix 1 to these reasons.

propositions.text: The only issue is whether the Decision is reasonable; adequacy of reasons alone is insufficient to set aside the Decision.
propositions.quote: In my view, the only issue raised by this Application is whether the Decision is reasonable. Contrary to Mrs. Khan’s assertions, the adequacy of the reasons provided in the Decision is not a stand-alone basis for setting aside the Decision.

propositions.text: Reasons must be considered with the outcome to determine reasonableness (Newfoundland Nurses case).
propositions.quote: Rather, those reasons must be considered together with the outcome in determining whether the Decision is reasonable (Newfoundland and Labrador Nurses’ Union v Newfoundland and Labrador (Treasury Board), 2011 SCC 62, at paras 14 and 22 [Newfoundland Nurses]).

paragraphs.summary: The court states the issue is whether the Decision is reasonable, citing Newfoundland Nurses that reasons alone do not suffice.

propositions.text: Mrs. Khan asserted her spouse was denied procedural fairness due to lack of interpreter at Interview.
propositions.quote: Mrs. Khan also asserted that her spouse had been denied procedural fairness based on the fact that an interpreter was not present at the Interview.

propositions.text: Mrs. Khan's counsel conceded the spouse should have raised the interpreter issue at the Interview, so it is no longer live.
propositions.quote: However, at the oral hearing, counsel to Mrs. Khan conceded that her spouse should have raised this issue at the Interview (Mohammadian v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2001 FCA 191; Kazi v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2002 FCT 733; Mohamed v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2014 FC 192). Accordingly, this is no longer a live issue in this Application.

paragraphs.summary: Mrs. Khan alleged procedural fairness denial due to no interpreter, but counsel conceded it should have been raised earlier, so issue is moot.

propositions.text: Review on reasonableness standard assesses if decision is within acceptable outcomes defensible on facts and law
propositions.quote: In conducting a review on a reasonableness standard, the Court will assess whether the Decision falls “within a range of possible, acceptable outcomes which are defensible in respect of the facts and the law” (Dunsmuir v New Brunswick, 2008 SCC 9, at para 47 [Dunsmuir]).

propositions.text: Decision must fit principles of justification, transparency and intelligibility
propositions.quote: the Court is required to consider whether the Decision fits comfortably within the principles of justification, transparency and intelligibility (Dunsmuir, above, at para 47; Canada (Citizenship and Immigration) v Khosa, 2009 SCC 12, at para 59).

propositions.text: Court assesses if decision explains why conclusion was reached and if conclusion is acceptable
propositions.quote: the Court will assess whether the Decision under review explains why the ultimate conclusion was reached, and whether that conclusion was within the range of acceptable outcomes described above (Newfoundland Nurses, above, at para 16).

paragraphs.summary: The court explains the reasonableness standard requires decisions to be justified, transparent, intelligible, and within acceptable outcomes defensible on facts and law.

propositions.text: Admission relied on by Officer to conclude spouse's direct participation in torture was insufficient
propositions.quote: Mrs. Khan submits that the alleged admission relied upon by the Officer in concluding that her spouse had directly participated in torture did not provide a sufficient basis upon which to reach that conclusion.

propositions.text: Circumstances of admission raise reasonable doubt about its occurrence
propositions.quote: She maintains that the circumstances in which the admission was allegedly made give rise to a reasonable doubt as to whether the admission was in fact made

propositions.text: Officer erred by not ensuring no ambiguity about the admission
propositions.quote: and that the Officer erred by failing to ensure that there was no ambiguity with respect to that admission.

paragraphs.summary: Mrs. Khan argues the admission used to conclude her spouse's direct participation in torture was insufficient, ambiguous, and doubtful.

propositions.text: Officer's conclusion of reasonable grounds to believe Mr. Khan directly participated in torture was not unreasonable
propositions.quote: In my view, the Officer’s conclusion that there were reasonable grounds to believe that Mr. Khan had directly participated in acts that amount to torture, and that such acts constituted offences referred to in sections 4 to 7 of the CAHWCA, was not unreasonable.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Officer's conclusion that Mr. Khan directly participated in torture was not unreasonable.

propositions.text: Reasonable grounds to believe standard is lower than balance of probabilities and serious reasons for considering
propositions.quote: The standard of “reasonable grounds to believe” that is set forth in section 33 of the IRPA contemplates a lower evidentiary threshold than what is contemplated by the standards of “balance of probabilities” and “serious reasons for considering” (Ezokola v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2013 SCC 40, at para 101 [Ezokola]).

propositions.text: Reasonable grounds exist where belief is based on compelling and credible information
propositions.quote: reasonable grounds will exist where there is an objective basis for the belief which is based on compelling and credible information (Mugesera v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2005 SCC 40, at para 114).

paragraphs.summary: The court explains the 'reasonable grounds to believe' standard is lower than others and requires compelling, credible information.

propositions.text: Mr. Khan's denial contradicted his interview statements; denial insufficient to reconsider preliminary inadmissibility conclusion
propositions.quote: the Officer noted that Mr. Khan’s denial that he had ever personally participated in, controlled or condoned torture was contradictory to what he stated in the Interview... such statements were not sufficient to warrant a reconsideration of the preliminary conclusion

propositions.text: Preliminary conclusion was Mr. Khan appeared inadmissible under IRPA paragraph 35(1)(a) for committing offences under CAHWCA
propositions.quote: That preliminary conclusion was that Mr. Khan appeared to be inadmissible pursuant to paragraph 35(1)(a) of the IRPA, because he had acknowledged that, as a member of the Pakistani military, he had committed acts that constitute offences referred to in sections 4 to 7 of the CAHWCA.

paragraphs.summary: The Officer found Mr. Khan's denial contradicted his interview and upheld preliminary inadmissibility for committing offences under CAHWCA.

propositions.text: Conclusion of reasonable grounds to believe Mr. Khan committed torture offences under CAHWCA was not unreasonable
propositions.quote: In my view, the conclusion that there were reasonable grounds to believe that Mr. Khan had directly participated in torture and had therefore committed acts that constitute offences under the CAHWCA referred to immediately above, was not unreasonable.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the conclusion of reasonable grounds to believe Mr. Khan committed torture offences was not unreasonable.

propositions.text: Mr. Khan's interview admission was compelling and credible due to detail, self-incrimination, and voluntary contrast with more egregious acts
propositions.quote: the admission given by Mr. Khan during the Interview was both compelling and credible... disclosure of those details constituted admissions against his interest... voluntarily contrasted the acts that he described with more egregious acts

propositions.text: Information had a 'ring of truth'
propositions.quote: The information provided by Mr. Khan during the Interview had a “ring of truth” to it.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Mr. Khan's interview admission compelling, credible, self-incriminating, and truthful.

propositions.text: No evidence of bad faith in CSIS security advice brief; brief clearly states Mr. Khan acknowledged use of certain interrogation techniques
propositions.quote: In the absence of any evidence of bad faith on the part of the senior member of CSIS who prepared the security advice brief, there is no reason to doubt the veracity of that brief... It very clearly states that Mr. Khan acknowledged “that he and other FIT members would slap, punch, use stress positions and force detainees to look at the sun to elicit confessions”

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no bad faith in CSIS brief, which clearly states Mr. Khan acknowledged certain interrogation techniques.

propositions.text: Credibility enhanced by Mr. Khan's additional detail that FIT handed detainees to police after confessions
propositions.quote: the credibility of this account is enhanced by virtue of the additional detail provided by Mr. Khan, to the effect that “the FIT would turn over the detainees to the police once they confessed or declared not involved in [sic] or knowledgeable of terrorist activities by FIT”

propositions.text: Additional detail clarifies interrogation techniques were by FIT, not police as asserted by Mrs. Khan and counsel
propositions.quote: that additional detail made it very clear that the interrogation techniques in question were conducted by the FIT, rather than by the police, as now asserted by Mrs. Khan and her counsel.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Mr. Khan's detail enhances credibility and clarifies interrogation was by FIT, not police as Mrs. Khan claims.

propositions.text: Officer reasonably found initial statements more credible than later disavowal by Mrs. Khan and counsel
propositions.quote: It was reasonably open to the Officer to consider the initial statements made by Mr. Khan to be more credible than the subsequent disavowal or clarification that was provided by his spouse and her counsel.

propositions.text: Initial statements made when Mr. Khan believed acts were not torture; disavowal made after inadmissibility apparent and only by Mrs. Khan and counsel
propositions.quote: initial statements were made at a time when Mr. Khan believed that the interrogation techniques that he described having personally used did not amount to “torture,”... disavowal or clarification was made only after it had become apparent that his earlier statements might render both him and his spouse inadmissible to Canada... disavowal or clarification was only made by Mrs. Khan and her counsel, as opposed to by Mr. Khan in an affidavit.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Officer reasonably preferred Mr. Khan's initial statements over later disavowal by Mrs. Khan and counsel after inadmissibility became apparent.

propositions.text: Evidence relied on by Officer was objective, compelling and credible to conclude reasonable grounds for Mr. Khan's direct torture acts
propositions.quote: the evidence relied upon by the Officer to conclude that there were reasonable grounds to believe that Mr. Khan had directly committed acts of torture... was objective, compelling and credible.

propositions.text: Officer's conclusion was within range of acceptable outcomes defensible on facts and law
propositions.quote: The conclusion reached by the Officer on the basis of that evidence was within the range of acceptable outcomes which are defensible in respect of the facts and the law.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes the Officer's evidence and conclusion on Mr. Khan's direct torture acts were credible and within acceptable outcomes.

propositions.text: Mrs. Khan asserts evidence raises reasonable doubt about Mr. Khan's torture acts
propositions.quote: Mrs. Khan’s assertion that the evidence gives rise to a reasonable doubt as to whether her spouse committed the acts of torture described in the Decision

propositions.text: Applicant confuses criminal standard of proof with Officer's standard of reasonable grounds to believe
propositions.quote: confuses the criminal standard of proof (beyond a reasonable doubt) with the standard of proof that the Officer was required to apply (reasonable grounds to believe).

propositions.text: Even if reasonable doubt exists, it does not preclude reasonable grounds to believe conclusion
propositions.quote: Even if the evidence relied upon by the Officer left open a reasonable doubt... that would not preclude... the conclusion that there were reasonable grounds to believe that he had committed those acts.

paragraphs.summary: Mrs. Khan argues reasonable doubt exists, but the court finds she confuses standards and reasonable doubt does not preclude reasonable grounds conclusion.

propositions.text: Officer's conclusion of spouse's complicity in torture was not justified, transparent or intelligible
propositions.quote: Mrs. Khan submits that the Officer’s conclusion that her spouse was complicit in torture, and therefore in crimes against humanity, was not appropriately justified, transparent or intelligible.

propositions.text: Decision did not specify which military divisions committed torture or link spouse to those divisions and acts
propositions.quote: she asserts that the Decision did not describe which divisions of Pakistan’s military had engaged in acts of torture, and that it did not address the link between her spouse and those divisions and acts.

paragraphs.summary: Mrs. Khan argues the Officer's complicity conclusion lacked justification, transparency, and failed to specify military divisions or link to spouse.

propositions.text: Court disagrees with Mrs. Khan's submission on complicity conclusion
propositions.quote: I disagree.

paragraphs.summary: The court disagrees with Mrs. Khan's submission on the complicity conclusion.

propositions.text: Complicity requires voluntary significant and knowing contribution to crimes against humanity
propositions.quote: To establish complicity in crimes against humanity, it is necessary to establish that an individual “has voluntarily made a significant and knowing contribution” to the commission of such crimes (Ezokola, above, at para 84; Talpur v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2016 FC 822, at para 21; see also Kanagendren v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2015 FCA 86, at para 21).

paragraphs.summary: The court states complicity requires a voluntary, significant, and knowing contribution to crimes against humanity.

propositions.text: Factors to assess complicity include size, part, duties, rank, time, recruitment and opportunity to leave organization
propositions.quote: In assessing whether an individual has made such a contribution to such crimes committed by an organization, consideration should be given to the following factors (Ezokola, above, at para 91): (i) the size and nature of the organization; (ii) the part of the organization with which the individual was most directly concerned; (iii) the individual’s duties and activities within the organization; (iv) the individual’s position or rank in the organization; (v) the length of time the individual was in the organization, particularly after acquiring knowledge of the group’s crime or criminal purpose; and (vi) the method by which the individual was recruited and his or her opportunity to leave the organization.

paragraphs.summary: The court lists factors to assess complicity including organization size, part, duties, rank, time, recruitment, and opportunity to leave.

propositions.text: Court will address each complicity factor below, combining duties and rank discussion
propositions.quote: I will address each of these factors below. For convenience, I have combined my discussion of the third and fourth factors.

paragraphs.summary: The court will address each complicity factor, combining duties and rank discussion.

propositions.text: Officer recognized Pakistan military's size and nature means many may not be responsible or complicit in crimes
propositions.quote: the Officer appropriately recognized that the size and nature of Pakistan’s military is such that many who have served with it may not have been directly responsible or complicit in the crimes against humanity that it is reported to have committed.

paragraphs.summary: The Officer recognized Pakistan military's size means many may not be responsible or complicit in crimes.

propositions.text: Officer did not explicitly mention FIT or other groups but was satisfied Mr. Khan was member of divisions responsible for abuses
propositions.quote: the Officer simply mentioned being “satisfied that [Mr. Khan] was a member of divisions within the army which were responsible for human rights abuses, including torture”

paragraphs.summary: The Officer was satisfied Mr. Khan was member of army divisions responsible for abuses but did not mention FIT explicitly.

propositions.text: Officer not required to mention FIT or other groups as information was provided by Mrs. Khan, counsel and Mr. Khan
propositions.quote: In the particular circumstances of this case, the Officer was not required to specifically refer to the FIT or to the other groups in the military in which Mr. Khan had worked.

propositions.text: Information about Mr. Khan's assignments and military divisions was provided in application, interview, and correspondence
propositions.quote: That information had been provided by Mrs. Khan, her counsel and Mr. Khan, either as part of the initial application, in the Interview, or in subsequent correspondence

propositions.text: Mr. Khan assigned to FIT 1992-1993 after years with Military Intelligence; was Lieutenant Colonel with Pakistan Rangers in Sindh
propositions.quote: Mr. Khan disclosed that he had been assigned to the FIT between 1992 and 1993, after having spent several years with Pakistan’s Military Intelligence [MI] group... Mr. Khan had been a Lieutenant Colonel with the Pakistan Rangers division in the Sindh province

propositions.text: Evidence indicated FIT, MI, and Pakistan Rangers committed torture and abuses in Karachi during Mr. Khan's stationing
propositions.quote: there was evidence before the Officer indicating that the FIT, the MI group and the Pakistan Rangers division had committed both torture and other human rights abuses, including in Karachi during the period when Mr. Khan was stationed there.

propositions.text: No dispute about Mr. Khan's involvement with these military parts; issues were their abuses and his complicity
propositions.quote: There is nothing in the CTR to suggest that Mr. Khan’s involvement with these parts of the military was a matter of dispute between the parties. Rather, the issues were whether those parts of the military had been involved in human rights abuses and torture, and if so, whether Mr. Khan had been complicit in those crimes.

paragraphs.summary: The Officer was not required to mention FIT explicitly; evidence showed Mr. Khan's involvement with military groups linked to abuses, which was undisputed.

propositions.text: Mr. Khan rose to Lieutenant Colonel in a long, successful military career
propositions.quote: The Decision noted that Mr. Khan had risen to the rank of Lieutenant Colonel over the course of a long and successful career in the military.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision found Mr. Khan rose to Lieutenant Colonel in a long, successful military career.

propositions.text: It was preferable for the Decision to address other leadership roles and duties Mr. Khan held
propositions.quote: It would have been preferable for the Decision to have specifically addressed some of the other positions of leadership that Mr. Khan had held in the military, together with some of his duties and responsibilities.

propositions.text: Given facts, addressing those roles was not essential as they were summarized in supporting materials
propositions.quote: However, once again, given the particular facts of this case, it was not essential that these matters be addressed in the Decision. This is because they were all summarized in the materials that were provided in support of Mrs. Khan’s application for a permanent resident visa.

propositions.text: Court may consider information in the CTR to assess reasonableness of the Decision
propositions.quote: it is entirely appropriate for the Court to consider the information in the CTR for the purposes of assessing the reasonableness of the Decision (Newfoundland Nurses, above, at para 15).

paragraphs.summary: The court found it preferable but not essential for the Decision to address Mr. Khan's other leadership roles, and may consider CTR information to assess reasonableness.

propositions.text: No dispute existed about Mr. Khan's ranks, duties, or activities except regarding human rights abuses and torture
propositions.quote: The CTR reflects that there was no dispute between the parties with respect to any of the ranks held by Mr. Khan, his duties, or his activities (other than as they may have related to human rights abuses and torture).

propositions.text: Details of Military Service showed Mr. Khan's ranks and duties from Captain in 1982 to Lieutenant Colonel in 2000
propositions.quote: The Details of Military Service that appear to have been provided in support of his spouse’s application state that, as Lieutenant Colonel between 1997 and 2000, Mr. Khan’s duties included “to ensure/assist local police in maintaining law and order.” ... Captain starting in March 1982.

paragraphs.summary: The court found no dispute about Mr. Khan's military ranks and duties, which were detailed in supporting documents.

propositions.text: The Decision found Mr. Khan's denial of participation in torture contradicted his interview statements
propositions.quote: the Decision observed that Mr. Khan’s denial of ever having participated in the activities ... is contradictory to what he stated in the Interview.

propositions.text: Mr. Khan admitted in the Interview to FIT's involvement in torture but later disavowed it
propositions.quote: Mr. Khan stated in the Interview that he and other FIT members engaged in those activities, which he now disavows but acknowledges would constitute torture

propositions.text: It was reasonable for the Officer to find the Interview statement more credible than the later disavowal
propositions.quote: it was reasonably open to the Officer to find that statement made during the Interview to be more credible than Mr. Khan’s subsequent disavowal or clarification

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision found Mr. Khan contradicted himself about torture involvement; the court finds the Officer reasonably preferred the interview statement.

propositions.text: CSIS brief states Mr. Khan revealed involvement with MI group linked to torture
propositions.quote: CSIS’s redacted security advice brief also states that Mr. Khan revealed that he had been involved with the MI group within the military.

propositions.text: Asian Human Rights Commission report cited MI group and Pakistan Rangers as agencies torturing detainees
propositions.quote: both the MI group and the Pakistan Rangers division are among the main agencies that keep persons incommunicado and torture them

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision noted CSIS and human rights reports linking Mr. Khan's MI group to torture practices.

propositions.text: CBSA report cited third party sources reporting torture by MI group and Pakistan Army during Operation Clean Up
propositions.quote: the CBSA report cited additional third party sources that reported on torture and other human rights violations perpetrated by the MI group and by the Pakistan Army, including during the 1992–1994 “Operation Clean Up” initiative

propositions.text: Mr. Khan admitted involvement in Operation Clean Up in Karachi
propositions.quote: Mr. Khan admitted having been involved in Karachi.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision found CBSA cited reports of torture during Operation Clean Up, in which Mr. Khan admitted involvement.

propositions.text: CBSA quoted US State Dept report noting credible human rights violation charges during Operation Clean Up
propositions.quote: the CBSA report quoted from the United States Department of State Country Report on Human Rights Practices for 1993, which noted that “Operation Clean Up” had sparked credible charges of human rights violations

propositions.text: CBSA quoted 1993 Amnesty International report describing widespread torture in Pakistan
propositions.quote: The CBSA also quoted a report from Amnesty International, published in 1993, which described torture by the police, the paramilitary and the military as having been endemic, widespread and systematic in Pakistan in 1992 and 1993.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision found CBSA quoted US and Amnesty reports describing widespread torture in Pakistan during early 1990s.

propositions.text: Evidence of FIT, MI group and Pakistan Rangers involvement in torture was objective, compelling and credible
propositions.quote: In my view, the above-mentioned evidence of the involvement of FIT, the MI group and the Pakistan Rangers in torture was objective, compelling and credible.

propositions.text: It was not unreasonable for the Officer to rely on that information to conclude those military parts engaged in torture
propositions.quote: It was not unreasonable for the Officer to have relied on that information, in concluding that those parts of Pakistan’s military had been engaged in torture.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the evidence of torture involvement by military groups credible and the Officer's reliance reasonable.

propositions.text: The Decision referred to open source information on military human rights abuses and Mr. Khan's membership in responsible divisions
propositions.quote: I am satisfied that that the above information was what the Decision was referring to when it stated that “[o]pen source information has reported that human rights abuses, including torture, have been perpetrated by the military in Pakistan,” and that Mr. Khan had been “a member of divisions within the army which were responsible for human rights abuses, including torture.”

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Decision referred to credible open source information on military abuses and Mr. Khan's membership in those divisions.

propositions.text: The Decision noted Mr. Khan served in the military from 1976 to 2000
propositions.quote: With respect to this factor, the Decision simply noted that Mr. Khan had served in the military from 1976 to 2000.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision noted Mr. Khan's military service spanned 1976 to 2000.

propositions.text: The Decision stated the army was Mr. Khan's chosen, long and successful career
propositions.quote: the Decision simply stated that “the army appears to have been [Mr. Khan’s] chosen career, which has been both long and successful.”

propositions.text: Mr. Khan's military career was voluntary; no suggestion it was involuntary
propositions.quote: It has not been suggested on behalf of Mr. Khan that any portion of his career with the military was not voluntary on his part.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision found Mr. Khan's military career was voluntary and long; no suggestion it was involuntary.

propositions.text: Officer's conclusion on Mr. Khan's complicity in human rights abuses was not unreasonable
propositions.quote: I am satisfied that the conclusion reached by the Officer with respect to Mr. Khan’s complicity in human rights abuses, including torture, was not unreasonable.

propositions.text: That conclusion was within a range of acceptable outcomes defensible on facts and law, considering CTR information
propositions.quote: That conclusion fell within a range of possible, acceptable outcomes which are defensible in respect of the facts and the law, particularly when regard is had to the information in the CTR to which the Decision alluded.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes the Officer's finding of Mr. Khan's complicity was reasonable and defensible on facts and law.

propositions.text: Considering undisputed information, the Decision fits principles of justification, transparency and intelligibility
propositions.quote: Considering the information that was provided by Mrs. Khan, her counsel and Mr. Khan, and that was not in dispute ... the Decision as a whole fit comfortably within the principles of justification, transparency and intelligibility.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Decision justified, transparent and intelligible given undisputed information.

propositions.text: The Decision addressed appropriate factors explaining the conclusion, supported by credible evidence
propositions.quote: the Decision explicitly or implicitly addressed the appropriate factors ... The findings described in the Decision were supported by credible evidence

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Decision addressed relevant factors and was supported by credible evidence.

propositions.text: High-ranking individuals may have knowledge or control over criminal acts (Ezokola, para 97)
propositions.quote: [a] high-ranking individual in an organization may be more likely to have knowledge of that organization’s crime or criminal purpose” and “may have effective control over those directly responsible for criminal acts.

paragraphs.summary: Ezokola states high-ranking individuals likely know or control criminal acts.

propositions.text: Longer membership increases chance of knowledge of organization's crimes (Ezokola, para 98)
propositions.quote: [i]t may be easier to establish complicity where an individual has been with the organization for a longer period of time” because this “would increase the chance that the individual had knowledge of the organization’s crime or criminal purpose

paragraphs.summary: Ezokola states longer membership increases likelihood of complicity knowledge.

propositions.text: Evidence provided compelling basis for reasonable grounds to believe Mr. Khan was complicit in torture by military groups
propositions.quote: Considered as a whole, the evidence ... provided a compelling basis for the conclusion that there were reasonable grounds to believe that Mr. Khan had been complicit in the torture

propositions.text: Mr. Khan voluntarily made a significant knowing contribution to crimes under CAHWCA sections 4 to 7
propositions.quote: that evidence established that Mr. Khan had voluntarily made a significant and knowing contribution to the commission of one or more crimes described in sections 4 to 7 of the CAHWCA.

propositions.text: This finding supported conclusion Mr. Khan is inadmissible under IRPA paragraph 35(1)(a), and Mrs. Khan under paragraph 42(1)(a)
propositions.quote: that implicit finding provided the basis for the ultimate conclusion that Mr. Khan is inadmissible to Canada pursuant to paragraph 35(1)(a) of the IRPA, and that therefore Mrs. Khan is inadmissible pursuant to paragraph 42(1)(a).

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes evidence supports reasonable grounds for Mr. Khan's complicity and inadmissibility under IRPA, affecting Mrs. Khan too.

propositions.text: Conclusions of reasonable grounds for Mr. Khan's complicity and personal involvement in torture were not unreasonable
propositions.quote: the conclusions that there were reasonable grounds to believe that Mr. Khan had been both complicit in, and personally involved in, acts of torture ... were not unreasonable.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the conclusions of Mr. Khan's complicity and involvement in torture reasonable.

propositions.text: The Application is dismissed
propositions.quote: Accordingly, this Application will be dismissed.

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the Application.

propositions.text: No serious question of general importance raised; no certification question
propositions.quote: Given that no serious question of general importance has been raised in this proceeding, there is no question for certification.

propositions.text: Judgment: 1) Application dismissed; 2) No question for certification
propositions.quote: THE COURT ADJUDGES THAT: 1. This application is dismissed. 2. There is no question for certification.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no serious question for certification and dismisses the Application with no certification question.
